rows: SYSTEM 3E vs 2x6 WOOD FRAME | 30- and 50-year life-cycle test for Riverknoll Renewal (Nov 26 2026)

Asked by the organizer: does System 3E pay back its extra upfront cost through lower upkeep, damage repair, mold, energy and insurance, and through faster unskilled dry-stack labor? 4. YEARLY SAVINGS OF SYSTEM 3E, per bed-year in 2026 $

What the wall system protects: the inside of exterior and party walls (no wood studs or cavity to rot, no drywall to punch through). What it does NOT protect: paint, floors, doors, cabinets, bathroom grout and caulk, and surface mold from steam and poor ventilation. Those cost the same either way, so they are left out.
Model v24 System3E tab: $6,594/yr base vs an R-22 wall; $2,801 vs R-25; $9,755 vs R-20 (all-electric heat pumps, $0.1966/kWh). A code wall with R-5ci sits near R-22 to R-25.

NPV of System 3E vs wood, walls only, 30 years at 5.15%

Base case (blocks stacked at the maker's speed, as the organizer decided Nov 26 2026): System 3E walls cost about $2,600 a bed more than code-level 2x6 wood walls with advanced framing, all in, and save about $133 a bed a year. On walls alone System 3E pays back in about year 28 (at 5.15%): about +$200 a bed over 30 years and +$1,300 over 50 (+$3,700 over 50 at 3%).

The whole System 3E building as model v24 has it (walls plus concrete plank floors) costs about $7,800 a bed more than a wood-frame building with wood floors, and the yearly savings do not pay that back within 50 years at 5.15% (-$3,900 a bed over 50 years; -$1,400 at 3%). The plank floors buy fire separation, sound and a wood-free building, not upkeep savings.

More than half the yearly saving is property insurance ($74 of $133 a bed-year), taken from a concrete-industry study at half its gap. If RIT's campus insurance does not price buildings by wall type, the saving falls to about $59 a bed-year and the walls never pay back.

The "idiot proof" point is real but small in money: plaster on block avoids wall holes and hidden wet walls (about $23 a bed-year). What students wreck most (paint, floors, doors, bathrooms, surface mold from showers) costs the same in either building.

Risk: if the first US crews are no faster than ordinary block laying, System 3E walls are about $13,800 a bed behind and never catch up (Pessimistic column). Ring beams, render and plaster still need skilled trades, so the schedule saving is about 1 to 2 weeks a phase and no phase opens a semester earlier.

The block price is still the biggest unknown: each $1 per sq ft of wall moves the result by about $660 a bed. A System 3E USA quote on the drawings, a crew productivity guarantee and an RIT insurance quote by construction type would settle it. A donated or discounted pilot supply would flip the walls to cheaper from day one.

First course in mortar, rest stacked mortar-free; "Everyone can build ... after a short training"; 145 m2 of walls 1 day vs 14; shell 3 vs 5 months; price incl. labor "similar to traditional methods"; grooves for wiring allowed; blocks must not be wet or frozen when laid; pH 7 perlite resists mold.
